title: Events, and the Advanced Cicerone
lead: Tap takeovers, flights and dinners, Michigan’s sample rules, then Cicerone’s third level.

sections.name: Tap takeovers

lines.label: In short
lines.text: One brewery, several taps, one night.

know: Start simple: 4–6 beers from a local brewer.
Order sixtels if the cooler is tight.
Tap the day before; have the rep brief staff.

sections.name: Samples and flights

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Free samples have limits; flights need ABV.

know: Michigan: free beer samples up to 3 oz, two per guest per day.
Paid flights aren’t covered by that limit.
Print ABV on the flight card.
sections.source: Michigan Liquor Control Code, MCL 436.2027 (legislature.mi.gov); NIH/NIAAA, “What Is a Standard Drink?”

sections.name: Dinners, verticals and cask nights

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Plan the beer like a menu.

know: Taste every beer at serving temperature first.
Sell a cask within three days.
sections.source: Brewers Association / CraftBeer.com, Beer & Food Course; Cicerone, Advanced Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 and exam page (cicerone.org)

sections.name: The Advanced Cicerone
know: 12 off-flavors on the tasting, plus oral exams.
sections.source: Cicerone, Advanced Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 and exam page (cicerone.org); Cicerone, Master Cicerone exam page (cicerone.org)

read.where: Operators interviewed by FSR Magazine: a first takeover of **4–6 beers** from one brewery is manageable; work with **local** brewers. Order **sixtels** when cooler space is tight, **tap the day before** so the chef can build pairings, have the **brewery rep brief** servers and bartenders, schedule on a **slow night**, and promote with the menu, tap handles, email and social media.
read.mixup: A takeover isn’t only for the brewery. Pick beers that fit our food.
read.sayIt: Tonight we’ve got six beers from one local brewery. Want a taste first?

read.bigIdea: Know the rules for free tastes.
read.where: Michigan’s Liquor Control Code lets an on-premises licensee give **free samples** only if it doesn’t charge: **beer up to 3 oz**, and no more than **two samples per guest in 24 hours**. That covers **free tastes**, not **paid flights**. For flights, print **ABV** on the card: four 5 oz pours of 5% beer are about **1.7 standard drinks**; at 8% it’s about **2.7**.
read.mixup: A flight isn’t a few free samples. It’s a paid drink, and it counts like one.
read.sayIt: I can give you a small taste of one or two before you decide.

read.where: For a **beer dinner**, the Brewers Association says get each beer’s ABV, style and ingredients, **taste** them at serving temperature (lowest ABV first), then order them to suit the dishes. A **vertical** tasting compares **2–6 vintages** of one beer at **2–3 oz** each. For a **cask night**, Cicerone says sell a cask within **three days** of tapping and clean cask lines weekly or at each cask change.
read.mixup: A vertical doesn’t have to go oldest to newest. Taste first and pair the years that show best.

read.where: The **Advanced Cicerone** needs a passed **Certified Cicerone**. It has an online **written** exam (multiple choice and essays), an in-person **tasting** with **12 possible off-flavors** (including acetic, chlorophenol, H2S, isovaleric, mercaptan and metallic), and two **oral** exams on styles and food pairing. You need **80%** overall and **75%** on tasting. Above it is **Master Cicerone**: a two-day exam, **85%** to pass. Our Advanced Specialist certificate is the restaurant’s; these titles only come from Cicerone.
read.mixup: Our Level 3 isn’t Cicerone’s Advanced level. It’s how we run our beer program.

sources: FSR Magazine; Michigan Liquor Control Code, MCL 436.2027 (legislature.mi.gov); NIH/NIAAA, “What Is a Standard Drink?”; Brewers Association / CraftBeer.com, Beer & Food Course; Cicerone, Advanced Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 and exam page (cicerone.org); Cicerone, Master Cicerone exam page (cicerone.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
